title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: Brute force to optimized: sorting first versus a hash set that only expands from true run starts.

blocks.text: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers that appear somewhere in the array, in O(n) time.

blocks.caption: A hash set enables O(1) presence checks; only genuine run starts trigger a forward walk

blocks.title: Analogy: The Longest Unbroken Run of Consecutive Ticket Numbers
blocks.text: Like sifting through a scattered pile of numbered raffle tickets to find the longest unbroken run of consecutive numbers present in the pile, regardless of what order the tickets were originally handed out in.

blocks.text: With no elements at all, there is no run to measure, so the answer is 0.
Before sorting, remember the problem explicitly forbids the O(n log n) that sorting would cost, so the real challenge is finding runs without ever putting the values in order first.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A hash set answers "is this exact value present" in O(1), which is exactly what is needed to check whether a run continues to the next consecutive integer, without ever needing the values sorted.

Observation 2: The naive way to use that set, starting a forward count from every value, would recount the same run once for every value inside it, since a run of length L would be independently walked L times, once from each of its members.

Observation 3: A value is only the true start of its run when the value one less than it is absent from the set; every other value inside a run has a predecessor present, and is therefore not a fresh starting point.

Observation 4: By only ever starting a forward count from a genuine run start, each value in the entire array is walked forward exactly once, as part of the one run it happens to start, or never, if it is not a start, keeping the total work across the whole array linear.

Whenever an expensive-looking nested walk would recount the same structure multiple times, look for a cheap "is this a genuine starting point" check that lets each element be processed exactly once overall.

This is the classic amortized-linear trick behind many hash-set based array problems: an inner loop that looks like it could repeat work is actually bounded, in total across all outer iterations, by the size of the input, once double-counting is eliminated by a starting-point check.
Sort the array first, then scan through it once, tracking the length of the current run of consecutive values and the longest one seen.

items: Sort the array.
Scan through it once, extending the current run whenever the next distinct value is exactly one more than the previous, and starting a new run otherwise.
Track the longest run seen.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: sorted(set(nums)) removes duplicates before sorting, since a repeated value would otherwise incorrectly look like it might start a new run of its own.
current resets to 1, not 0, every time the run breaks, since the value at the current position always counts as at least a run of length 1 by itself.
best is updated with the running maximum after every extension of current, so the longest run is captured even if a later, shorter run follows it.

blocks.text: Sorting correctly brings consecutive values next to each other, so scanning for runs afterward is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated entirely by the sort.
Space: O(n), for the sorted copy.
Limitation: the problem explicitly asks for O(n) time, which sorting alone cannot achieve, since sorting itself is already O(n log n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Sorting solves the problem correctly, but it does more work than necessary: it establishes a total order across every value, when all that is actually needed is "does the next consecutive integer exist", a question with only a few possible answers per value. A hash set answers that exact question in O(1) without ever needing a global order. The remaining risk is wasted, repeated work: walking forward from every single value would re-trace the same run multiple times. Restricting forward-walks to only genuine run starts, values whose predecessor is missing from the set, ensures every value is walked forward as part of at most one run, the one it actually starts, collapsing what looks like nested work into a true single pass over the array.

Put every value into a hash set for O(1) membership checks. Then, for every value, only begin counting a run starting from it if that value minus 1 is NOT in the set, meaning it is genuinely the start of some run, not the middle of a longer one that would be double counted. From each true start, count forward as far as consecutive values continue to exist in the set. Since every value is only ever counted once, as part of the one run it truly starts, the total work across every run combined is O(n).
A hash set of every value, only expanding forward from values that are genuine run starts.

blocks.caption: Optimized: a hash set of values, expanding forward only from genuine run starts

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since every value is only ever visited as part of counting the one run it genuinely starts.
Space: O(n), for the hash set.

Every value in the array belongs to exactly one maximal consecutive run, and that run has exactly one true starting value, the one whose predecessor is absent. Since the run-start check filters out every non-starting value before any forward walk begins, each run is only ever walked forward once, by its own unique starting value, so the sum of every inner loop's total iterations across the entire outer loop can never exceed the total number of distinct values, keeping the overall work linear.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Condition","Meaning"],"rows":[["Predecessor is not in the set","This value is a genuine run start; begin counting forward from here"],["Predecessor is in the set","This value belongs to a run that some earlier, smaller value already starts; skip it"]]}

items: set(nums) deduplicates and enables O(1) membership checks in one step, replacing the sorted array's ordering with direct presence lookups.
The run-start check is the single line responsible for keeping the algorithm linear overall, since without it every value would attempt its own full forward walk.
The inner while loop only runs for as long as the current run genuinely continues, stopping the moment the next consecutive value is missing.
best is updated with the running maximum after each run start finishes its full forward walk, capturing the true length of that specific run before moving to the next candidate start.

blocks.text: The key insight is the "only start from a true run start" check, which guarantees that even though the inner while loop looks like it could repeat work, the total work summed across every outer iteration is still linear, since every value participates in exactly one run's counting.

items: Omitting the "predecessor not in the set" check, which would recount the same run multiple times, once from every value inside it, turning the algorithm quadratic in the worst case, such as one giant run covering the whole array.

Forgetting to deduplicate before or during processing, which does not break correctness here since a hash set naturally deduplicates, but is worth being aware of when reasoning about the algorithm's true behavior.
Iterating over the original array instead of the deduplicated hash set when doing the run-start check, which does not break correctness but does redundant repeat checks for duplicate values.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["An empty array","Returns 0 immediately, since there are no values at all to form any run"],["An array with duplicate values","The hash set naturally collapses duplicates into a single entry, without affecting the correct run length"]]}

items: Explain explicitly why the total work stays linear despite the nested-looking loop: every number is only ever the starting point of counting once, precisely because of the run-start check.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the longest run or streak of consecutive values, in O(n)" points toward a hash set for O(1) presence checks, plus a run-start filter, predecessor absent, to guarantee every value is only ever walked once overall.

items: How would you also return the actual sequence, not just its length? Track the starting value alongside the best length found, then reconstruct the run by counting upward from that starting value once the best is known.

What if the array were streamed and could not fit in memory all at once? A pure hash-set approach needs the whole set available; an external, sorted-merge based approach, or a different data structure with bounded memory, would be needed instead.

How would this change if "consecutive" meant consecutive even numbers, or some other fixed step, instead of integers exactly 1 apart? The same hash set and run-start technique applies directly, just checking membership at value plus or minus the step size instead of plus or minus 1.
Same "hash set for O(1) presence checks" foundation as Two Sum and Contains Duplicate, applied here to detect chains instead of single matches or repeats.
Same "only start from a genuine starting point to avoid redundant work" insight as sliding window problems that must avoid re-expanding an already-explored window.
Same amortized-linear-total-work argument used to justify many union-find and graph traversal algorithms, where a nested-looking loop is bounded overall by marking visited or started elements.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force (sort based): O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (hash set with run-start check): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Hash set membership checks combined with a run-start filter to guarantee linear total work
Core Idea: Only begin counting a consecutive run from a value whose predecessor is absent from the set, ensuring every value is walked forward as part of at most one run
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n), for the hash set
Most Important Observation: A forward-walk that looks like it could repeat work stays linear overall once restricted to genuine run starts
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Only start where the chain truly begins: no predecessor, no problem
